analysis.one_liner: Raises the royalty, rent, and bid rates oil and gas companies pay to drill on public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the federal onshore oil and gas royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75% was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in February 2020 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law charges oil and gas companies 12.5% of the value of what they pump from public land, plus low per-acre rents and a $2 minimum bid at lease auctions. This bill would raise the royalty to 18.75%, raise rents and minimum bids, charge companies a fee when they nominate land for leasing, and adjust all of those dollar amounts for inflation every four years. The extra money would go to the federal treasury, which shares it with states. The bill never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal, state, and local taxpayers, who would collect more money for oil and gas taken from land the public owns; and future budgets, which would no longer be locked into decades-old rates that never rise with inflation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who own the public lands

how_it_helps.text: Raises the onshore oil and gas royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75%, so the government keeps a larger share of the value of oil and gas produced from public land [S3].
Raises the minimum bid at lease auctions from $2 to $10 per acre and raises annual rents from $1.50 to $3 per acre in the first years of a lease and from $2 to $5 per acre afterward [S3].

Adds a new fee of at least $15 per acre for companies that submit an 'expression of interest' naming land they want leased, and requires the Interior Department to adjust all of the per-acre rates for inflation at least once every four years [S3].
Requires a National Academy of Sciences study, reported to Congress within 3 to 5 years, on how well the Interior Department collects and audits these payments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that lease federal land would pay higher royalties, rents, bids, and fees; some of those costs could be passed on through energy prices, and some drilling might shift off federal land.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

drawbacks.text: Companies would face materially higher costs on federal leases; the royalty increase alone is a 50% jump over the current 12.5% rate, which could reduce how much companies bid to lease federal land or push them toward state and private land instead [S3].

If fewer companies lease federal land, the government could collect less total revenue than expected even at higher rates, and lower federal production could mean higher prices for consumers who buy oil and gas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is simple: the public owns this land, and rates set in 1920 had not been updated for inflation. Raising them would bring federal terms closer to what states like Wyoming charge. The honest tradeoff is that higher rates may mean less federal drilling activity, so the extra revenue is not guaranteed and some cost could reach consumers. But the current rates are a known bargain for leaseholders, and the bill's inflation adjustment would keep future rates from lapsing again.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on February 25, 2020, joined by Sen. Chuck Grassley, its only cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that continued leasing federal land at the old 12.5% royalty and low rents; taxpayers forgo the additional revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies still drilling under old rates

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise federal oil and gas royalty, rent, and bid rates.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democrat and one Republican behind it, but no votes were ever taken on it, so the record shows only the bipartisan sponsorship.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal public land
industries.note: The bill would raise the royalty they pay from 12.5% to 18.75%, quadruple the minimum lease bid, and roughly double annual rents and add new fees. The current below-market rates effectively let companies buy public resources cheaply, so their interest in keeping them runs against the taxpayers who own the land.

industries.industry: State governments with federal lands (through revenue sharing)
industries.note: Federal onshore royalties are shared with states, so higher rates would mean more money for state budgets, schools, and roads in energy-producing states.
